definition.text: The idea that people should control their own food systems, including how food is produced, distributed and consumed.

facts.text: Food security is about access to enough food, whereas food sovereignty is about who controls the food system and how food is produced.
Via Campesina coined the term in 1996; the 2007 Declaration of Nyeleni, from delegates of 80+ countries, defines it as peoples' right to healthy, culturally appropriate, ecologically sound food.
As of 2020 at least seven countries had written food sovereignty into their constitutions and laws.

Advocates say the Green Revolution raised output without solving hunger because it ignored access to land and economic power; critics say the movement rests on wrong assumptions about subsistence farming.
Seed sovereignty is a related right to breed and exchange open-sourced seeds, argued for on biodiversity and climate resilience grounds as well as food justice.

definition.text: A species living outside its native range after being brought there by human action, also called alien, exotic or non-native.

facts.text: Introduced species that establish and spread are naturalized; only those that spread widely or quickly and cause harm to the environment, health, resources or economy are invasive.
Introductions are intentional (for economic gain, recreation or fixing environmental problems such as erosion) or accidental, as with rats on ships or marine organisms in ballast water.
Non-native crops and livestock account for 98% of US food.
Whether an exotic will become invasive is seldom understood at the start.
